speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on May 14, 1982, the federal PC party moved in part the following motion which was opposed by the Liberal and NDP spokesmen, "that the government immediately implement a moratorium on all metric related prosecutions and action be taken to abandon compulsory metrication in Canada."

subsubtopic: CALL FOR HOLDING OF GENERAL ELECTION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, added to the many knowledgeable voices predicting an even worsening economy as a result of the mismanagement of this country, is the view of officials from the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce who, only yesterday, forecast unemployment reaching a record level of 12 per cent of the work force, and a continued gloomy economic future for the nation.
Canadians themselves clearly understand what all these financial experts are saying, that this government has caused and is continuing to cause our financial woes and is doing little to solve them. This understanding by the average, financially pressured Canadian, is reflected in the latest Gallup poll which shows the government at an all-time low in popular support, 19 percentage points behind the Progressive Conservatives. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Erie (Mr. Fretz):
That the government show some concern for the state of this nation and some respect for the plight of Canadians by putting the welfare of both ahead of its desire to cling to power, and immediately call a federal general election, or at least the three byelections.

subsubtopic: RECOGNITION OF HEROISM OF RAOUL WALLENBERG-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in March, 1944, Nazi Germany partially occupied Hungary and dispatched Adolph Eichmann to organize the deportation of the
20004

last substantial population of Jews within Nazi influence. Eichmann quickly completed what he proudly called "a deportation surpassing every preceding deportation in magnitude". Some 437,000 Jewish men, women and children were sent to concentration camps on 148 trains between May 14 and July 8, according to a Nazi report.
A young Swedish diplomat by the name of Raoul Wallenberg, arrived in Budapest in July on a rescue mission and in the ensuing months saved perhaps as many as 100,000 persons, including many Canadians of Hungarian origin. Arrested in 1945 by the Soviets, reports still persist that he is alive. Today, August 4, would be the seventieth anniversary of his birth. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean) and the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie):
That this House, on the occasion of Raoul Wallenberg's seventieth birthday, recognizes his heroic deeds on behalf of all humanity and urges the Government of Canada to continue its efforts to obtain information about him from the Soviet Union.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance, and it concerns the more than 15,000 man-years and the jobs we have lost in the Canadian shipbuilding industry, which have affected employment in the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia directly. Yesterday an industry spokesperson pointed out that the contention of the minister last week that the shipbuilding industry in Canada is uncompetitive is competely false. Earlier a report prepared for another government department by a government-hired expert also indicated that what the minister contends is false. The report indicated that the Canadian shipbuilding industry is quite competitive.

protesting the bombardment up to that point of West Beirut and saying that the process should be seen as reflecting a deep and growing concern in the Canadian Parliament and public over the impact upon civilians of the Israeli bombardment of Beirut.

speechtext:

Oral Questions
foul-up at a Toronto incinerator, and found their way into the hands of individuals who were arrested just last month by the Toronto metro police. subsubtopic: DISAPPEARANCE OF QUANTITY OF SEIZED DRUGS

Madam Speaker, 1 do not know who the spokesman is supposed to be, but 1 do not agree with that statement. I can assure the House that 1 have already asked the RCMP for a full report on the matter. 1 will see, when 1 get the report, if any further investigation is justified.
1 understand from the investigation to date that, of the
13.000	pounds of drugs which were sent to be burned, it is now established that only 35 pounds are unaccounted for. This is far from the $10 million value shown in The Toronto Star. subsubtopic: MR. MAZANKOWSKI-TABLING OF GILSON REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I understand that the minister has just tabled the government's response to the Gilson report. Again we have witnessed in this House a practice which has become increasingly frequent during this session, that is, the failure of ministers to make announcements of substantive policy measures in this House. Instead they have merely tabled a document or issued a press release outside the House. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has demonstrated today once again his contempt and disregard for this institution and for all hon. members of the House of Commons.
This is the third occasion on which the minister has, in dealing with a question of very substantive policy, namely the future of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates in this country, avoided the House of Commons. On February 8 he issued a statement in Winnipeg and that was a substantive statement of policy. The members of the House of Commons did not have an opportunity to respond; they did not have an opportunity to question the minister or to seek clarification on a very important and complicated subject. The opposition had to use an opposition day to get this issue on the floor of the House of Commons.
On June 28 when the Gilson report was released, once again the House of Commons was circumvented. A statement was made in Winnipeg; the minister held a press conference; once again the Members of Parliament and this House of Commons were not involved.
Today we have a statement that has been tabled by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). We do not know what it contains but we do understand that it is the government's response to the report of the Gilson task force. What is further rubbing salt into the wounds of all hon. members is the fact that the minister is going to go outside of this House of Commons and hold a press conference. I believe that is contemptuous and totally disregarding the role, the responsibility and the obligations that we have as Members of Parliament. He merely tables the report today. There is no statement, no opportunity for opposition members to respond. There is no opportunity to seek clarification. He is doing it by press release by tabling a document and holding a press conference outside of this chamber.
We all know this same Minister of Transport a year ago waited until Parliament recessed to make a very substantive announcement with respect to VIA Rail. This has been a habit with this minister and I must say it has been shared as well by other ministers of this government.
I am sure that you realize, Madam Speaker, that the issue of the Crowsnest Pass freight rates is a very fundamental and important issue to the people of western Canada and particularly to the farmers, the producers and the grains industry of
western Canada. We all acknowledge that this government does not have any members in this House west of Winnipeg, but that should be no reason why this Parliament should be left out in the cold. We on this side of the House find, the action of the Minister of Transport contemptible. We believe that it constitutes an abuse of the rights and privileges of all members of this House of Commons. We believe it impairs the ability of each and every one of us to discharge our responsibility and to serve our constituents and our region.
I ask you, Madam Speaker, as one who presides over this chamber and who has the responsibility of ensuring that rights and privileges of all Members of Parliament are preserved, to seriously look into this matter and take the necessary steps to see that this practice cease and desist.

Madam Speaker, on this issue I think the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) is perfectly right. Since about 1975 we have had nothing but a litany of bypassing Parliament on the issue of the Crowsnest Pass statutory grain rates. We have had nothing but a total ignoring of the Hall royal commission by the government. We have had a total refusal by the government to let the Transport Committee-could it be because there are no Liberals from the prairies?-deal with this matter. The minister stacks the deck with organizations that he knows are opposed to statutory grain rates, namely, the private enterprise section of the grain industry. He refuses to consult the grain producers by way of a referendum to give them a choice whether they want the recommendations of Gilson or Mr. Justice Emmett Hall.
This business of using press releases and statements tabled in the House indicates to me that the minister does not want to make a statement on motions so that members of the opposition parties can respond. Instead of that, we have to work in our offices or down in Room 130S to respond to something that is so fundamental to the whole country, as well as western Canada.
Surely the minister should be bigger than he has been in dealing with this matter and should not continue to run around behind the backs of Members of Parliament in dealing with this issue on the last day of this House sitting.

Madam Speaker, I will be very brief. This bill to amend the Railway Act is intended to increase safety in Canada of the operation of trains. At the present time the railways in the United States have a law that railway workers operating trains will not work more than 12 hours if they
require rest. When they cross the border to come into Canada, that act is no longer in effect. Sometimes they work as many as 20 and 25 hours without obtaining rest. subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in rising to participate in debate at the third reading stage of this bill I want simply to say at the outset that "six and five" is an exciting opportunity for Canada. It has been recognized by Canadians as an exciting opportunity to lead us on the path of recovery in the country.
We know that the problems which afflict the economy are far-flung and that their origins can be found in a complexity of causes, international as well as national. We know that a large part of the solution can be achieved only as a result of actions taken beyond the borders of Canada, particularly in the United States but also in other countries of the western world and, indeed, the world in general. However, we also know that if Canada is to be in a position to benefit from recovery as soon as that can be achieved, we have to do those things which will enable the maximum recovery to occur here and the maximum benefits to accrue to our people. Specifically, that means reducing the rate of inflation in this country.
1 do not think there are hon. members who seriously would contend that the rate of inflation in Canada, running so far above that of the United States, is not the major problem and the major threat that is unique to Canada. We have in common with the United States, Germany, England and other countries a tragically high level of unemployment. We are afflicted by the same high interest rates those other countries have. And, as has been said many times, the dominance of the economy of the United States over those of other countries means that the change in interest rates must, to a large degree, be initiated there.
But what this bill is directly aimed at is that problem which is more grave in Canada than it is in the United States, and that is the problem of a rate of inflation that is higher here than in the area in which we sell our goods. If we are to sell our goods in that area, we must compete against United States domestic production. That is the situation with regard to many Canadian products being sold into the American market.
I think I speak safely when I say that the vast majority of the Canadian public recognize the threat inflation constitutes. The interesting factor in relation to this bill, perhaps the most important bill with which we have dealt in this session-and, indeed, for some period of time- is the opportunity it presents to Canadians to aim their efforts directly at combating inflation. It is not that the statutory provisions of this bill alone, by any means, affect a large enough part of the economy to bring about the amount of reduction in inflation that will be necessary in order to maximize the opportunity for Canadians in the recovery period. Rather, it sets a good example. It shows the way, the way that Canadians are already seeing and the way to

August 4, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
which Canadian workers, businessmen and professional people react positively in vast numbers all across the country.
It is interesting to contrast the different positions of the two opposition parties on this bill. As I have heard and read the remarks of the official opposition, they are to the effect that restraint is good. The opposition is in favour of the principle of restraint but members say they cannot go along with the bill because it is presented by the government and the system is such that they have to try to make the government look bad and disagree with what it is doing. Since they cannot disagree with the principle of the bill, they try to attack the credibility of the government and spend their time trying to find some group not covered by the six and five as fully as the government intended.
This has been an interesting exercise. As they sought to do that, to their surprise, instead of defending any legitimate exception that has been found, the government has reacted by agreeing to plug such loopholes because it believes all Canadians must share in the sacrifices that are necessary if the program is to work.
I understand the approach of the opposition. That is its role. It is not its function to make the government look good. Even in difficult times when it is important to the country to have a program which can provide possibilities for recovery, as this one can, it is hard for a member of the opposition to say he is 100 per cent behind the program. Hon. members opposite know in their heart of hearts that it is an important program at this time for the country. They hear what the people in the country are saying. Perhaps a great number of people are surprised at how well the public of Canada is reacting to the principle of six and five-to the principle that in general we have to limit what we can take out of the economy if we are to create a climate in which it can grow.
The challenge for the minister who introduced this bill and for all of those on the treasury benches-and I recognize that there are difficulties in the challenge-is to establish our credibility. The challenge is to establish that we are not only reducing the increase in salaries for civil servants to six and five per cent over the next two years, but in the same way that we have cut back on the salaries of Members of Parliament and cabinet ministers, we are seeing to it that the regime, if you like, of six and five applies in every way it possibly can. Certainly it is a question of using leverage.
I was surprised at the criticism made by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The Prime Minister said that taxpayers' dollars are used for programs to provide special assistance to industries that have particular problems-he called that leverage-and that we ask in return that they join this crusade, since they are getting this benefit of special assistance, in helping to cut back by undertaking to keep prices and wages within the six and five margin in their operations. I think that is a very legitimate undertaking. I think it is the responsibility of government to do everything possible to see that this voluntary system works as it applies to the private sector in the
country and that as many organizations as possible are encouraged to join and make that element of sacrifice that is necessary if we are going to build for the future in this country and if we are to solve the economic problems that the western world shares with us at the present time.
I was vastly encouraged by the polls conducted by the Gallup organization that showed that something like 80 per cent of the Canadian people would be prepared to take a decrease in pay, let alone a limitation on the amount of increase, in order to work together in the common cause of building a better tomorrow for our country. That is the Canadian way and perhaps we should not be surprised that the public is often ahead of the politicians-it is their world and their country. 1 am delighted that so many large and small companies and business associations have already endorsed the principle of six and five. I think that is important.
Let me come back to the question of credibility. I want to say to members of the House and to the people of this country that those of us who are in government are determined to do everything we can to see to it that within the government's operations there are no unnecessary exemptions to this program and that everyone shares in the sacrifice that needs to be made.
1 would be quick to admit that obviously, as someone said about wage and price controls in the mid-1970s, they constitute rough justice. They do, because if a person is living on a more comfortable level of income then they can stand the gaff of restraint and can cut back to a greater degree than someone who has a limited income. Still, the percentage approach, in dollar terms, hits the person in the higher-income bracket much harder than it does other people.
There has been a lot of debate on this bill. I think hon. members opposite, whatever their approach may be to the exact terms of the bill, will have to agree that the minister has shown a commendable flexibility in relation to its terms. It is not a bill that has been returned for third reading unchanged from its original form. Rather, it has been altered in a number of ways, thus demonstrating the flexibility of the minister and the government. We are not so concerned about the exact wording of the bill; what we are concerned about is that we achieve legislation that will bring about a restraint program within the government service that is an example to the rest of the country and that will achieve the desired goal. There is flexibility in relation to bargaining wages, benefits and nonmonetary items.
I could talk about other changes that have occurred but 1 am satisfied with the reaction of the various organizations in the country and with that of people generally. Hon. members opposite know well what I am talking about when I say that the reaction of the public to this program is very positive.
There is a mood in this country that in my \9Vi years in public life I have not seen before. There is a mood of being prepared to share, of being prepared to make the sacrifice and
August 4, 1982

of recognizing that we have to get on with seeing to it that Canada does not lag behind the other countries of the world in building a more prosperous tomorrow and overcoming the incredible economic problems which we have today.
1 have said a word about the reaction of the official opposition to this bill. I have spoken about the fact that members of the official opposition do not question the principle. They have tried to find loopholes or have suggested that we were not serious about it or that there would be exceptions and so on, because they have to talk about the bill.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport

speechtext:
Yes. My hon. friend and so many of his associates are stuck right back in the 1930s. Ideologically they have never escaped the 1930s, nor have they recognized that these times are different. The Regina manifesto lives forever in their hearts and in their minds so that they cannot deal with today's situation.
I want to say to members of the New Democratic Party that they, unfortunately, have structural encumbrances preventing them from dealing with the wisdom of this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: Can you define that?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext:
The New Democratic Party never looks better than when it is defending the widows, the poor, the unemployed or the unorganized. As a former Minister of Labour I am fully cognizant of the problem of the unorganized who by far make up the vast majority of the workers, in fact, nearly two thirds of them. They are the people who suffer particularly from inflation. It is the widows, the unemployed, the people on pensions and those with special disadvantages who suffer from inflation. There is no question about that at all. If you look, Mr. Speaker, through the speeches made by members of the New Democratic Party at the different stages of this debate, and there have been ten or 11 of them, you would think that inflation did not exist as a problem, that all we had to do was go blithely along having an inflation rate 6 per cent or 7 per
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
cent higher than the United States and that that poses no problem to Canadians.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: Who has been in government all those years?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: My goodness, Mr. Speaker, when members of the New Democratic Party start to yell, it means we are getting close to the bone.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: You have hit a soft spot.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext:
I have not started to get close to the bone yet. But let me say that the New Democratic Party never looks better than when its members are speaking for the disadvantaged, the unemployed or the poor. However, they have a structural encumbrance in this issue which prevents them from properly representing those they claim to be their clientele. Do you know what they have to decide, Mr. Speaker? They have not done so in this debate but they have to decide whether their primary clientele is going to be the poor, the people who have less in this world and need government help to a greater degree, as we recognize on this side, or whether their primary clientele is the structural alliance that they have with a certain portion of the trade union movement of this country. They are not even allowed by that structural encumbrance to represent the views of the individual members of those unions, let alone the unorganized-the 66 per cent of the ordinary workers- because they cannot displease that small minority who are union leaders. They are a very integral part of their organization, a very important controlling part of their organization. How can they stand and say: "We believe in sharing. We believe all Canadians should share and, therefore, those who are organized and who have the clout to take from the economy more than the economy can properly give at this time should not be allowed to do so but should be restricted to six and five also?"
Do you know what the union leaders say to them, Mr. Speaker? They say: "We are the business agents and if we are not able to go out and bargain and get more and more wages, and if there is going to be some restriction even for a short period of time, then how can we justify our existence to our members?" That is the problem which they confront. Consequently, with this bill the New Democratic Party is in a quandary.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: We are the only ones who voted solidly against this bill. This bill split the Tories and the Liberals.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: They are solid all right, from one end to the other. 1 only want to say that they are blocking their ears to what the people of the country are saying. I do not mean to suggest that members of the NDP are a dull lot because there are some very, very able people in that party. As long as the people can be assured that no one is cheating and that everyone is going to sacrifice, that is what they want.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext:
The reason the New Democratic Party cannot do that is that the minority, that part which provides so much

August 4, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
of the financing for the NDP, the organized-not all organized labour but part of organized labour in this country-are telling them they cannot do that.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: What do the banks tell you to do? Are they telling you to keep interest rates high? Is that it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: What is the result? The result is that the NDP has to say no and oppose the bill. Its members have to say no to the widows and to the poor. But they know who is affected most by inflation. They know which people inflation hits the hardest. Members of the NDP should look at speeches they have made in the past about that problem. I might say that the constant chatter that emerges from the New Democratic Party benches mean that we are even closer to the bone now and that they are really concerned about the conflict in which they are involved.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext: You have hit a soft spot.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext:
Yes, as the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) has said, I think we have hit a soft spot. I appeal to members of the NDP. They are elected here as Members of Parliament to represent all of their constituents, not to represent the union leaders of some of the unions of this country. I ask them, as we come to third reading of this bill, to think about the 60 some per cent of the workers of the country who are unorganized and who do not have the ability to get continuous increases in ever larger amounts to keep up with and get ahead of inflation. I ask them to recognize the lack of justice in a system that allows inflation to go unchecked, when those who have the benefit of clout can negotiate renewals and agreements which overcome that problem. But the pensioners, the unemployed and the unorganized of the country are not in positons to do so. That is why they should support this bill.
Inflation attacks those in our society least able to defend themselves, such as the elderly and others on fixed incomes, but it also attacks our valued social institutions like hospitals, schools, churches and charitable organizations.
We have heard, by my count, 11 NDP speakers at second reading and several more at committee stage. None of them has really come to grips with the problem of inflation. They either want to ignore it altogether or declare, as an article of faith, that wages have nothing to do with inflation. I want to say clearly that I am not one who believes that inflation, as it exists in the country, was originally caused, in its latest upward spurt, by wage demands. Certainly I do not believe that it was caused by wage settlements in the public service. However, I do believe that from the point a year and a half or so ago when wages caught up with inflation and started edging ahead we have entered into the extremely dangerous period where wage increases feed on the already existing inflation and spiral it upwards, with devastating problems in the groups of society which I mentioned. Thus we have a situation where wages become a very important part of what must be restrained if we
are to achieve success in combating inflation and making a better economic opportunity for Canadians.
In that circumstance the government concluded that because federal public servants are in the service of the public they have a responsibility to set an example and to help show the way. I do not think it is simply because of the fact that it can be argued that they do not face the same danger of lay-off as people in the private sector where, suddenly, there is no money to operate a business and the jobs are gone. I suppose some could say that that is a factor, but I think it is simply that they are a part of government and the public expects an example from government. As long as the example comes from everyone in government, then I believe, as we are seeing, the rest of the country is prepared to follow.
I want to appeal even yet-and I guess it is in vain-to hon. members of the New Democratic Party to recognize not just their responsibility but everyone's primary responsibility to the unorganized, the elderly and pensioners who cannot combat inflation by negotiating a big new increase.
For us to abandon the bill, for us to follow the system that we have, means we would simply end up with the organized and the powerful moving further and further ahead and the squeeze on the rest of our citizens becoming greater. This is why I think the bill is good.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks-and I am now at the conclusion of them-the bill does not begin to touch enough of the over-all economy to bring about what must be achieved in bringing inflation down to 6 per cent. It is not designed to do that. It is designed to show the way, to provide an example by government. My gosh, every day we pick up newspapers or go out into the streets of our home cities and find example after example of how people are reacting. I dare say the minister is surprised-I am-at how positively the Canadian public has reacted to this and what has been the response. You fellows over there in the New Democratic Party should get your heads out of the sand and recognize the real world out there. The NDP should recognize their primary responsibility, overcome their structural encumbrance with their affiliation with trade unions and payment from the trade unions, and recognize that they have a responsibility to the unprotected and the unorganized.

speechtext: Like the pensioners you limited to 6 per cent.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OFCANADA
speechtext:
That is right, like the pensioners. They have brought in their reinforcements over there. Now they have another member who is feeling a little upset by the remarks being made, but I will not repeat them for the hon. member's benefit; this is a serious matter. I appeal to the NDP to act responsibly, in the interests of the nation, and to stop playing politics to curry favour with union leaders.
The passage of this legislation is an important signal to the Canadian public that we are serious in this restraint program.
I appeal to all hon. members, as they go forth from this place and return to their constituencies in different parts of the country, regardless of their political affiliation, to recognize inflation. Let us be honest and say that inflation is a very big

expectations, I believe the fact that the country is strong, worthy and has a long-term stability to which it can look forward has been true during the past 14 years. 1 want to read part of the most moving testimony heard by the miscellaneous estimates committee. I believe it sets the appropriate tone for this debate. This was testimony given by Dr. Carl Beigie, who is the chairman of the C.D. Howe Institute, one of the most noted policy analysts in North America. I would like to read what he said about the state of the country. This is not what a member of the House of Commons said, not a Liberal, Conservative or New Democrat. It was a policy analysis by a person whose job it is to report and analyse the appropriateness of policies of government.
I should say to the House that the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) was present at the committee hearings. He will know that of all the witnesses who appeared, Dr. Beigie was the only witness who met with the spontaneous applause of all the members of that committee. There is no magic formula, no theory, no formula, no overwhelming historical evidence which exists to tell us how we can get out of the situation we find ourselves in.
He was really expressing, on behalf of Canadians and, I hope, on behalf of Members of Parliament, that somehow this program, as inadequate as it is, as has been admitted by the Secretary of State, is at least one which will set the mood. But he warned us that there is no magic formula. He also expressed the necessity for hope that that would happen. Then he said:
-there is no easy way to bring down a high rate of inflation. The difficulty of the task of bringing down inflation becomes greater, the longer high inflation persists.
He went on to state:
Canada's evolution as a society has been marked by the progressive expansion and extension of freedoms. If this evolution is to sustain a forward momentum, individuals throughout this nation must begin to display greater awareness that expectations for more rights, and particularly the rights resulting from improved standards of living, can only be satisfied with the acceptance of more responsibilities for the nurturing of the collective interest.
Canadians may, or may not, have become soft. What happens with the passage of time will determine the answer to that question. I am convinced, however, that many of those Canadians who value individual liberty have been asleep. They have been lulled quietly into this state by tales of an abundance of natur.al resource wealth which could keep us, Canada, from experiencing severe

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members for giving me consent. I assure the House leader of the New Democratic Party that I will do my best to stay within the 30 minutes, as he has requested.
I would be remiss if I did not begin my remarks by making a brief reference to the various interventions made by members opposite. They made reference to letters recently written by me to the editor of a major national newspaper. I very much enjoyed their interventions. I do not know whether their utilization of my letter to the editor will encourage or discourage future writings on my part. However, I owe them a word of thanks for the free publicity they have given me.
In a serious vein before embarking on my speech, I want to make reference to interventions regarding some mysterious plot or plan on the part of the government to prevent me from appearing before the special committee which dealt with this bill. The inference was that somehow I was prevented from appearing.
Nothing could be further from the truth in that regard. Let me put the record straight. The invitation to appear before the committee was extended for days that 1 had been scheduled to be out of town. Otherwise, both the minister responsible for the status of women and myself would have been very glad to appear. I am referring to the dates after July 26. Having put that matter to rest, I now want to say the following in relation to the bill before us.
This bill establishes wage restraint by statute in the federal public sector, and by example in the rest of the economy. It is not labour legislation; it is part of the economic policy arising from the last budget. However, the bill has implications for the conduct of collective bargaining and for those terms and conditions of employment that are established in the democratic process.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, labour legislation on the federal statute books today is rooted in acts introduced since the turn of the century by successive Canadian governments. As we all know, these governments were mainly Liberal governments. One stream of legislative development has given us an impressive array of protective provisions which establish important labour standards. These standards include minimum wages, hours of work, vacations and maternity and other special leaves. They also provide for occupational safety and health regulations. These provisions compare well with standards established elsewhere in the industrial world. A second stream of legislation has produced two labour relations statutes
governing collective bargaining and related matters in federal industries and the federal public sector of Canada respectively.
Our collective bargaining laws contain many positive features to promote labour stability. The concept of protecting the public interest in collective contract disputes was first introduced some 75 years ago under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, with William Lyon Mackenzie King as his deputy minister of labour. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act of 1907 established a concept of public investigation of labour disputes before strike or lockout action could be undertaken. That concept remains an important element of our current laws.
Subsequent additions to our labour legislation have provided orderly procedures for the recognition of trade unions by employers as bargaining agents and for the acquisition of bargaining rights. Elsewhere such matters are sometimes resolved only after bitter recognition strikes.
Perhaps most importantly, our system is built upon the stable foundation of the fixed-term, enforceable collective agreement. The parties are required to honour their obligations to each other throughout the life of their agreements. Grievances arising as to the interpretation or application of the agreements must be settled, without resort to work stoppage, by arbitration or some other means. This feature of our system is perhaps most frequently remarked upon by foreign visitors. Some come from countries where such grievances can lead to sudden and damaging strikes.
In these circumstances I am more than cognizant of the precedent-setting nature of the bill which is presently before us for consideration. I have wrestled long and hard with its impact upon a paramount feature of our approach to industrial relations, namely, the fixed-term, enforceable collective agreement to which I have just referred. Not to have reflected seriously on that aspect of the bill would have been unworthy of the office of Minister of Labour.
Frankly, the most disturbing element of the bill for labour legislation is the override feature. In cases where a wage increase would otherwise have been due on or after June 29 of this year it will be disallowed and a statutory amount will replace it. Instead of a freely negotiated wage increase and other mutually agreed to changes in terms and provisions being allowed to prevail, the law will substitute a prescribed increase and effectively require the status quo to be observed with respect to other items and conditions of a compensation plan.
I am sure that hon. members of this House will share my awareness of the fixed-term agreement as the cornerstone of our industrial relations system. The importance of the sanctity of such agreements within that system cannot be overestimated. Only extraordinary and serious circumstances can justify the extraordinary and serious step of setting aside agreements which have been freely negotiated or which have been concluded on the basis or arbitral awards.

In the past this House has consented to adopt rapidly legislation to terminate specific labour disputes. Such steps have been taken only in emergency situations after very careful consideration. Frequently, support for such legislation has been forthcoming from all parts of the House. We have established, therefore, that there are times when the national interest must override the rights of particular groups in collective bargaining. What we are now considering is legislation which follows the same reasoning, but on a broad front.
The government has concluded that against a background of worldwide economic difficulties, domestic circumstances do warrant the extraordinary and serious measures proposed in Bill C-124. 1 wholeheartedly endorse this conclusion and, as a member of the government, I stand ready to do all within my power to implement the proposals before us today.
Reactions to our proposals in some quarters suggest that not everybody has realized the seriousness of the current economic situation and its effect upon all Canadians. Some appear not to have accepted the need for rapid implementation of the extraordinary measures proposed. 1 am encouraged, however, to see signs that important elements of the business and labour communities comprehend the gravity of our circumstances. Regrettably, too many workers in the resource and manufacturing sectors have had the seriousness of our economic problems brought home to them in a very personal way. Employees in the service sectors are also-again regrettably- becoming affected to a significant degree.
The need to start ratcheting down inflation and inflationary expectations has therefore become urgent. Wages in the federal public sector and federally administered prices are two key areas in which the Government of Canada can act directly to achieve that end. With respect to wages, it would be unthinkable to let stand agreements which had been negotiated in the hope of better economic times, now that it has become clear, in Canada and elsewhere, that the better times are not just around the corner. Indeed, the longer action is postponed, the further off these better times will be.
The government's aim is not to undermine collective bargaining. It is a system which, generally, has served us well. It can continue to contribute effectively to important economic processes, such as income distribution and the achievement of improved productivity. However, it is a system which, by its very nature, including its largely decentralized application, cannot be expected to respond rapidly to the economic circumstances with which we are faced today. The government therefore proposes to intervene to ensure that a response from the system is forthcoming.
By interrupting collective bargaining rights the government is doing two things. First, it is indicating to the nation the gravity of the economic situation and the urgent necessity to put our economy on the road leading to recovery. Second, with this bill it is asking federal public sector employees to make a sacrifice and to accept the idea of increases limited to 6 per cent and 5 per cent in order to convince other levels of government, provincial and municipal-and with them the private sector-of the necessity of doing the same. When 6 per cent is the norm, everybody in the nation will be the winner. When inflation, too, reaches 6 per cent-a goal nobody disagrees
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
with-we will have completed the first step towards economic recovery.
The proposals before us today, with one important addition that I intend to deal with shortly, touch only the federal public sector, that is, the Public Service of Canada and federal Crown corporations and their wholly-owned subsidiaries. The federal public sector is not as readily affected or as immediately responsive to market forces as the private sector. Even Crown corporations, which are more oriented toward the marketplace than the traditional public services, are sheltered to some extent.
By limiting the wage increases of persons who, in the broad sense, are federal public sector employees, the government is taking direct action in an important sector of the economy. We are determined to do all in our power to persuade, coax, and induce others, including private sector employers and unions, to take similar steps. If collective action in support of restraint is not forthcoming, the cost of not making the effort will be borne by all sectors of the economy.
The addition to the scope of the bill, to which I referred earlier, involves an incursion into the private sector. The Canadian Pacific Railway and several private short-line railroads operating in federal labour jurisdiction have developed a long-standing bargaining relationship with their Crown-owned counterparts. This voluntary industry bargaining pattern has been encouraged and nurtured, for many years, by officers of Labour Canada in concert with the railway unions and companies.
For all practical purposes, the private sector railways bargain jointly or in tandem with the Canadian National Railways and its short line subsidiaries for contracts with unions representing the respective groups of operating and non-operating railway employees. Over the last few months, the companies and unions bargained responsibly and eventually concluded two-year renewals of their collective agreements which were scheduled to run until December, 1983.
When the substance of Bill C-124 became known, it was abundantly clear that the long-standing bargaining relationship between the public and private sector railways could be jeopardized. Indeed, the railway unions themselves brought the anomalous situation forcibly to the government's attention. Allowing the anomaly to persist would have created untenable stresses in railway labour relations, and within the unions themselves. Removing the anomaly requires following one of two starkly contrasting options: exempt the CNR and its
45,000	or so employees from the restraint program, or include the CPR and its employees in the program.
To have removed the CNR and its employees from the program would have significantly undercut the intent and coverage of the bill. Exempting a major Crown corporation engaged in a vital economic activity would have belied the seriousness of this government's commitment.

Naturally, we would not have expected the railway unions to campaign publicly for including the CPR in the program. However, Canada's railway workers have a long tradition of successful and responsible labour relations. Now that the government has decided to count CPR in, there is not a shadow of doubt in my mind that the railway unions will respect the law in a responsible manner.
I am equally confident that all employees destined to come under the federal public sector compensation restraint program proposed in Bill C-124 will accept the need for the program and its basic wisdom.
Because of the insidious effect of inflation in eroding real earnings the government is launching extraordinary measures, including the public sector compensation program-this bill- aimed at bringing the scourge under control.
The seriousness of our problems is obviously recognized by many in this House. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) made clear his support for the principle of restraint on wage increases when he addressed the bill last Friday. However, he could not accept the limits which are imposed on other aspects of collective bargaining for compensation plans.
He accepts the need for extraordinary measures but he would hamstring the restraint program. Instead of a simple and uniform approach, he would establish a complex and hard-to-administer program. It is questionable whether what he proposes would find much favour among those to be covered by this bill.
As to the proposals made by the NDP, earlier this afternoon the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) made a very eloquent intervention in which he exposed the dilemma they face in relation to the constituency that they are going to protect and serve.
It is well known to anyone who has engaged in labour relations in Canada at the provincial and federal levels that collective bargaining is the most democratic method yet devised, in a free and growing economy, to protect real incomes, to ensure improved working conditions and to reward real productivity gains with real income growth. However, in a troubled economy the government has to act in the interests of everyone, from the pensioner to the minimum wage earner, from the unorganized worker who cannot command high wages in the marketplace to the unemployed, from the export manager engaged in a price war with foreign competitors to the worker whose job depends on that market.
A responsible government today cannot shrink from the task of planning on behalf of all Canadians. With this bill we are asking one group of Canadians to make a temporary sacrifice for the benefit of all.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia), because I can see why the members of the government who sat on the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates which considered this bill kept him hidden. I can see why from June 30, when the government introduced this bill, until August 3, not one word was heard from the Minister of Labour. I can
understand why the Minister of Labour can no longer be considered a defender of the rights of workers in this country.
What the minister did in this House was to read a statement that was obviously prepared by somebody to defend this government's position. In his speech he referred to the quote we have used a couple of times in this debate. It is from a letter which the minister wrote to The Globe and Mail. He stated that the right to strike is one of the important cornerstones of a free and democratic society. That minister did not say the same thing today in this House.
Further on in the letter we read that, "there is clearly room for greater co-operation between unions and employers and that Parliament has entrusted to Labour Canada the responsibility for assisting in the development and maintenance of constructive relationships." What this minister has done in front of us today is to indicate that he has sold out the very principles that he wrote about in his letter to The Globe and Mail. That minister can no longer be trusted by labour. If that minister wants his cabinet spot, he should find another place because he certainly does not belong where he is. He cannot represent labour.

Yes, for the government. It is amazing to note that until tonight, on the last day of the debate on what the government calls a major piece of legislation, the cornerstone of economic planning for the next two years, the present Minister of Labour was not trusted to deliver the government's case. That is probably an indication of what is thought of the Minister of Labour. It is an indictment. It is saying that the minister is not capable of performing the duties which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) appointed him to do.
In his short speech, the Minister of Labour talked about the serious nature of the economic situation that we are in. He talked about the extraordinary situation that Canadians are
August 4, 1982

facing. He is right. We have been saying that throughout this debate, just as my leader and other members of our caucus have been saying for the last couple of years. We recognize the serious situation in which the Canadian economy is in. But this measure will not do one thing for the unemployed of this country. It will not do one thing to solve the inflation problem that we have. This measure will not do one thing to lower interest rates in this country. Interest rates are the real problem because they are killing the Canadian economy at this time, not the wages of Canadian workers, nor the wages of public service workers who receive lower increases than those in the private sector. The government has attacked not the villain but the victim.
This bill will do nothing to prevent business bankruptcies. It will do nothing to prevent farm bankruptcies. It will do nothing to restore this economy of ours. The government knows that. We have quoted a number of times before from the government's leaked document, a copy of which our leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), obtained. It reads in part:
-a program of consultation and public relations aimed at changing public attitudes and expectations would be useful-even though 'the main advantage of the program would be that it would enable the government to be seen doing something about inflation and to lay part of the blame for inflation on the private sector.'
The government admitted in its own document that it was a public relations job. The government admitted that the program would actually do very little for the state of the Canadian economy and the government admitted that it is an attempt to cast blame on others, and yet the Minister of Labour defended that policy in this House.
In a speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) and in speeches made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston), who spoke a number of times on this issue, the government has called for co-operation. The government has asked that other sectors of the Canadian economy co-operate with it in this program. But the government is not willing to co-operate with other sectors of the economy. The only people the government met prior to this legislation were representatives of the Business Council on National Issues, the leaders and chief executive officers of the largest corporations in this country. That is the group that called for a 7 per cent wage control program in the public sector. That is the group which fathered this legislation. That is the only group which the government consulted prior to this legislation being introduced. The Canadian Labour Congress, the Public Service Alliance of Canada, other public service unions, the premiers, municipalities, small-business people were all brought in after this legislation was introduced. They were not consulted beforehand. Their co-operation was an afterthought by this government.
If this government were really serious in having a united program which would lower interest rates and keep energy prices from going up 31 per cent in the next year, it would have taken advantage of the time it had. But it did nothing for six months about the state of the economy. It did nothing from

the November 12 budget to the June 28 budget. This government could have used those six months to work with other representatives of the various sectors of Canada's economy. They would have said, as members on the opposite side are now saying: "We have a very serious situation at this time." The government should have been saying that for the last six months, instead of downplaying the economic calamity that faces Canada. For the last six months the government downplayed the problems that we face. Then all of a sudden at the end of June the government decided that the situation was so terrible that it had to do something overnight. The government wasted six months. Now the government expects public servants and other wage earners across this country to make a sacrifice, a sacrifice about which the government has not consulted them.
I spoke earlier about the fact that the Minister of Labour was a no-show at the committee which studied the bill. I mentioned previously that the minister responsible for the status of women did not show. The Liberal majority on that committee prevented her from showing at that committee. Last night we had a situation where the minister responsible for the status of women voted against a New Democratic Party motion which specifically would have allowed the negotiation of paid maternity leave. That motion had only one other operative clause, that is to say, that paid maternity leave should not be included in any 6 per cent or 5 per cent compensation package. Not only do we have the Minister of Labour who no longer represents labour, but we have the minister responsible for the status of women who does not represent the women of the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not mind having my speech interrupted for that particular motion.
Before the interruption, I was talking about the facts that the Minister of Labour does not represent labour and that the minister responsible for the status of women has forsaken the women of the country. Now I should like to turn to the party which is supposed to represent opposition to government. I should like to start by quoting the comments of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), who said in an inverview which was published in The Citizen and in a number of other South-am newspapers across the country that if he were Prime Minister:
I would reject controls. And I wouldn't allow my PMO to be issuing rumours that they were coming in while I was saying that they weren't. I think that controls won't work.
Last night the Leader of the Opposition and members of his party rose and supported the government on a controls program. I find that that contradiction indicates that they are not in opposition to the Liberal Government of Canada; they are in coalition with the government.
There was one motion on which they voted with us and against the government. It was the one which rolled back the present salaries of the staff of Members of Parliament and Senators. Also it was a motion on which a number of government members supported us and on which a number of government members abstained. The motion to which I am referring was carried by the government side by 27 votes. At the time there were 41 Conservative members missing from the House.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: And six NDP members.

speechtext:
The Conservative Party has the sole responsibility for keeping the Liberals in power as of last night. The government was telling its backbenchers that the amendment to restrict the salaries of their staff was a matter of confidence in the government. Despite what government members may have personally felt about how hard their staff worked or about how hard they struggled to survive on their incomes, for the most part they supported the motion of the President of the Treasury Board. However, there were enough of them who were not present in the House. Also there were enough of them who had the courage of their convictions to support the New Democratic Party in opposing it. However, with that matter on the record, a matter of confidence in this government, which could have brought it down last night, 41 Conservatives were missing. They hid. They kept the Liberals, that arrogant group of incompetents, in power.
August 4, 1982

From now on do not let any Conservative say that it is the NDP who keep the Liberals in power, because last night they had their one and only opportunity since February 18, 1980 to get rid of the Liberals and they blew it. Let us remember that. There were 41 Conservatives out of the House, and the Liberals are still in power today. They will remain in power because the Conservatives will do the same thing on major economic issues such as interest rates.
We have heard from the Leader of the Opposition and the member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) saying that they have no other solutions. With respect to the energy issue there is the acknowledged fact that the Conservative Party would do almost the same thing as the Liberals.
Despite the fact that the Leader of the Opposition said that he did not believe in controls and he would not implement them because they would not work, the Conservative Party voted with the Liberals last night, ensuring that the Liberals will not be defeated on the only weak part of the bill which Liberal backbenchers would not support; the only Achilles heel which the Liberals had, and upon which the Conservatives could have acted. But the Conservatives hid.
When it came to the final vote last night we watched the Conservatives line up again in support of their Liberal masters despite the fact that they spoke against salary cuts to our workers, despite the fact they voted in favour of paid maternity leave, with the exception of five Tory members whom I wish I could identify, and despite the fact that the Liberals defeated their amendment with regard to the Human Rights Commission, and their amendment on collective bargaining.
When we are faced with any major and significant economic issue in Canada, the Liberals and Conservatives are one and the same. It is a Liberal coalition with the Conservatives that is keeping the country in the terrible and degrading economic situation in which it is today. Those two parties are responsible for high interest rates. They are responsible for the high rate of inflation in the country. They are responsible for the 1.3 million officially unemployed, and who knows how many more unemployed in this country.
This country is facing very serious economic problems. Our party has discussed those problems. We have talked about the need for restraint. The hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), the hon. member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish), who served on their respective committees in the House, have raised specific examples of government waste. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has talked about the public purse being ripped off by the oil corporations in this country. We have discussed all of these issues. We have warned that by allowing energy rates to increase 31 per cent in the next 18 months, inflation will be fueled even further and it will add to the killing of the Canadian economy. Bankruptcies will rise for farmers and businesses. Yet we have been attacked by the Liberal-Conservative coalition who have said that we are not concerned about the economy.

We are concerned about the economy. That is why we have kept the House here since the end of June, through all of July and into August.
We regret that this bill will do nothing to help our economy. We regret that the Liberals and Conservatives have ganged up to zap the workers in what has been described in a government document as "a public relations program" to blame the private sector for the country's ills. We regret that the result of this program in two years will still be a high cost of living, at much higher than 6 per cent, since energy prices are being allowed to increase 31 per cent and interest rates are so high that the cost of living must go up. There will still be bankruptcies and more unemployment, more shutdowns, more people losing their homes, and more people leaving the resource-based communities. It is so unnecessary.
Since the Conservatives take an anti-labour position on most issues, and the Minister of Labour has enunciated his position on labour which is basically capitulation to the President of the Treasury Board, and he will do nothing to protect the legal rights of workers, Canadians have before them a public relations effort in the form of this bill which will do absolutely nothing to help them or the Canadian economy.
I said earlier that the government has wasted the last six months when it had the opportunity between the budget of November 12 and the budget of June 28 to develop a program in co-operation with Canadians from all walks of life. We recognize, as do other members and most Canadians, that the present program will do nothing. Therefore, I will momentarily move a motion to give this bill a six months' hoist.
If this government and its collaborators in the Conservative Party are genuinely concerned about the state of the economy, they will support this motion. They will not use those months to create further hatred, to make one group of Canadians the scapegoat, to hurt those who will be retiring in the next two years and be forced to live on smaller pensions as a result of this bill, or to prevent women from getting negotiated paid maternity leave. In those six months the government would have the opportunity, if it were serious, to begin discussions and negotiations to seek the kind of compromise which is typically Canadian, and to ensure that we have a program which will resolve what the Minister of Labour called the very serious economic conditions facing us at this time. We will not have a program whereby Ian Sinclair, through the co-operation of this government, can zap his workers and prevent them from ever negotiating for more than 6 per cent and 5 per cent increases. We will have a program which will not outlaw collective bargaining. We will have a program which does not give the government the right to break the collective agreements which it may have signed as recently as two months ago.
In other words, if the motion which I am about to present does pass, and if the Conservatives and Liberals can vote on principle and on the future of this country, then perhaps-and it is not for sure-we can solve our problems by Canadians working together, through agreement by Canadian men and

It is hard for some one who will lose his home next month because of high mortgage interest rates to agree that he must take a 6 per cent and 5 per cent increase over the next two years. It is hard for a businessman to recognize that his whole purchasing community, his customers, will have limited incomes, will spend less in his store, and that he will go bankrupt. It is hard for those Canadians to sacrifice more. But there are many Canadians in support of this program, including the Ian Sinclairs and the de Granpres who have salaries, respectively, of $550,000 and $600,000 a year. There are other groups that have that right and ability to sacrifice. As a result, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke (Mr. Parker):

Mr. Speaker, I will cut short my remarks in order to help everyone even if I have responsibility for the bill.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased with this opportunity to speak to a bill that has been the subject of debate during the past few months and is, in fact, a very delicate subject for Parliament because it concerns amendments to the Criminal Code regarding relations between persons. I believe that what we are proposing today in the House represents part of the work that the House and the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs have undertaken in the course of their consideration of Bill C-53, and we have thus succeeded in resolving half the problem, at least. I therefore wish to thank all the members of this House for having made it possible to dispose of this bill this afternoon, and I wish to thank all those who testified before the committee and all hon. members who sat for many hours, especially during the marathon sitting last Wednesday, which went on quite late into the night.

To turn to the particular provisions of the bill, first, an effort has been made throughout the bill to degenderize the Criminal Code provisions relating to sexual offences in keeping with the equality rights guaranteed by the Charter of Rights. The few remaining references to a male person or a female person will be dealt with when we amend the child exploitation provisions of the code.
Second, Section 244 of the code, defining assault, is amended by the addition of a new subsection to make it clear it is not
Criminal Code
consent to an assault where there is submission or lack of resistance because force is used against the complainant or a third party, such as the child of the complainant, or threats or fear of force is used against the complainant or a third party, or fraud is employed, or exercise of authority such as in an employer-employee relationship.
Third, a further provision has been added, as a result of the Supreme Court decision in Pappajohn, to require judges to instruct juries to consider the reasonableness of any grounds for belief by the accused that the complainant consented to the assault.
Fourth, under the category of sexual assault we are, first, creating a hybrid offence, with the possibility of an indictable offence with a maximum of ten years, or summary conviction, with six months' maximum for minor touching cases. This first level offence will cover everything from touching to forced sexual intercourse with a minimum of violence.
At the second level, sexual assault with a weapon, or with threats to a third party, or causing bodily harm to the complainant will call for a sentence of up to 14 years.
Finally, at the third level of seriousness, there will be a further category of aggravated sexual assault for wounding, maiming, disfiguring, or endangering life; this offence will carry a maximum of life imprisonment.
Among the further reforms proposed by this bill, I want to mention that corroboration of a complainant's testimony will no longer be required for conviction. This will make the law of sexual assault consistent with other types of crime.
The doctrine of recent complaint, developed from the old idea that a woman must raise a hue and cry against her attacker in order to be believed, will be eliminated.
No questions shall be asked about a complainant's prior sexual history with a person other than the accused, except as rebuttal to evidence led by the Crown, to prove identity, or where the other sexual activity was occurring at the same time.
Finally, I want to underline that "spousal immunity" is being eliminated by this bill. Women are not the chattels of their husbands, and sex without the consent of both parties is as unacceptable within marriage as it is outside of marriage.
With respect to that there will be an amendment to clarify it even further. In the committee hearings I was of the view that clarification was not needed, but members of the committee felt that it should be clarified. The words proposed before the committee were not acceptable, in my judgment as Minister of Justice, but since that time we have worked out new words. I understand that a motion will be presented by the hon. member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), which will be seconded by my parliamentary secretary because of the work he did. I have accepted this motion.
Two new offences are created by Sections 250.1 and 250.2 to deal with the problem of child custody battles between

August 4, 1982
Criminal Code
parents. Section 250.1 makes it an offence for a parent to take his child in contravention of an existing custody order made by a court anywhere in Canada. Section 252.2 applies where there is no custody order as such, but one parent has had de facto custody of the child. In this case, consent of the attorney general of the province or his local representative will be required for prosecution.
Defences are provided for where the absconding parent has the consent of the custodial parent, and also for the rare case in which the absconding parent can persuade a court that his motive was to save the child from "danger of imminent harm".
1 have proposed an amendment myself for Clause 19 that would clarify Section 246.6(1 )(c). There was long debate about past sexual activity. My amendment will make sure that if there is any question about it it will be related to the incident of the moment. It will not permit delving into the person's history. As we discussed in committee there might be circumstances where, if there is activity involving many people at the same time, it has to be described because it might be related to the sexual activity of that person with another person in those circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say that, today, we have made considerable progress. We have received proposals and suggestions from a number of organizations which appeared before the comittee. I particularly wish to thank all the women's organizations in Canada which took a very special interest in the proceedings. We introduced this bill in the House a year and a half ago, and we have made considerable progress in our attempts to reach a consensus. The issues are basically very complex and that is why, when I appeared before the committee, I purposely took a very flexible approach and said that I was open to all kinds of suggestions. I was so flexible that opposition members accused me of not knowing what I wanted. I wanted to experiment by giving the committee the greatest possible flexibility while remaining personally responsible for accepting or not accepting certain amendments. I was a little disappointed by the results, because at one time I found that people held this against me and claimed that I did not really know what kind of reforms I wanted to make. Nevertheless, I have no regrets, and we are going to continue this fall because there are still some problems to be cleared up, including the issue of child pornography. I think this is a point we must clear up once and for all. Some people insisted that the problem was not a major one yet, but I am convinced that the problem exists. This has been proved by witnesses who appeared before the committee, and even if it is only in its initial stages, I think it should be stopped immediately. That is why I was so disappointed when we were unable to reach an agreement. Incidentally, the member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) said that in 1976 and 1977, the committee had already recommended reforms in this area. I hardly think that, at the time, the committee was basing its views on assumptions only. It was in the light of this report by the House committee that I agreed to introduce these proposals, and we shall get back to
them if the session continues this fall, and otherwise, we shall introduce the measures again. Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank everyone who worked on this legislation. However, today I am somewhat disappointed that amendments have been proposed. When we were discussing ways of resolving this problem in committee, I agreed there would be no amendment and that we would be coming here without amendments. My concept was that any changes could be made in the fall, because we would then be considering the same kind of bill and improvements could be made to the bill at that time. However, amendments were proposed, so 1 also proposed one, that is, I accepted the amendment on spousal immunity. In fact, I produced the text that will be presented by the member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), and I also accepted further amendments which were proposed by the official opposition.
There were other amendments which I unfortunately could not accept. As Minister of Justice, I have to consider certain proposals, and I am thinking of the member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer) who made some representations. He was a little disappointed that I did not accept an amendment he had discussed with my parliamentary secretary. Unfortunately, it touched on an area where we want to ensure that sexual offences and sexual assault are defined in a new Criminal Code in such a way that it is easier for the person concerned to press charges. The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Cambridge seems quite reasonable, at first. However, one criticism that could be levelled against the amendment is that it goes against what we are all trying to achieve, namely, make it easier to make complaints and easier to make recommendations. If I had accepted the amendment, I think we might have regressed in relation to the joint commitment we made, especially vis-a-vis the women's groups, which insisted that corroboration should not be compulsory in order to find a person guilty of sexual assault. I can assure the hon. member that we shall get back to this if necessary.
I would like to thank my colleague, the Minister responsible for the Status of Women who is in the House today and who has been following this debate very closely, as well as the member for Saint-Michel (Mrs. Killens), both of whom have been keeping at me on the subject for several months. 1 am thankful to them for having exerted this pressure. I want to thank the members of the opposition for their co-operation. I wish to thank the chairman of the committee, the member for Arthabaska, no, for Lotbiniere (Mr. Dubois). Mr. Speaker, the town of Arthabaska happens to be in his riding and that is why i made a mistake. I especially wish to thank my parliamentary secretary, who this last week has been working very hard to get a consensus. We made a small bet, and I said I did not think we would be successful. In fact, I said this on purpose, to get him going, and I am very grateful that he won his bet.
